name: Risperidone (Risperdal)
summary: Second-generation antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar mania, and sometimes used off-label for severe agitation or as an add-on for treatment-resistant depression or OCD. Effective, but carries real risks: weight gain/metabolic changes, movement side effects, high prolactin, and a boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.
description: Risperidone is an atypical antipsychotic that can reduce psychosis, mania, severe agitation, and irritability. It can be sedating for some people and activating for others (akathisia/restlessness). It also has a higher-than-average chance of raising prolactin (sexual side effects, menstrual changes, breast symptoms) and can cause movement side effects (stiffness, tremor, restlessness). In older adults with dementia-related psychosis, antipsychotics increase the risk of death—risperidone is not approved for that use.
patient_summary: Risperidone can help with psychosis, mania, and severe agitation, and it’s sometimes used as an add-on when depression or OCD won’t budge. People often notice less intensity, fewer intrusive symptoms, and more emotional steadiness—but side effects can be the dealbreaker (weight gain, sleepiness or restlessness, stiffness/tremor, and sexual or hormone-related changes). It also carries a serious boxed warning in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis: higher risk of death.

primary_indications: Bipolar I Disorder (maintenance; long-acting injectable forms)

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved for schizophrenia. Often improves hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, disorganization, and agitation. Most people notice early changes in 1 to 2 weeks, with fuller benefit over 4 to 6 weeks.

FDA-approved for acute mania/mixed episodes and for maintenance of bipolar I disorder (including certain long-acting injectable formulations). Early calming can happen within days, but mood stabilization continues over 1 to 2 weeks.
Sometimes used as a low-dose add-on to an antidepressant when depression is not improving (augmentation strategy).
Sometimes used as augmentation to an SSRI/SNRI or clomipramine in treatment-resistant OCD.
May be used for severe acute agitation when psychosis is driving the agitation and safety is at risk. Route and setting matter; dosing is usually short-term and symptom-driven.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity (eg, anaphylaxis, angioedema) to risperidone, paliperidone, or any component of the formulation

efficacy_response.patient_text: For schizophrenia, many people feel some early improvement in 1 to 2 weeks (less intensity, less agitation), with a more complete response over 4 to 6 weeks. For acute mania, early calming may show up within days, with continued improvement over 1 to 2 weeks.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral: Rapid and well absorbed; food does not meaningfully change absorption
pharmacokinetics.onset: Agitation (ODT): median time to calm ~70 minutes (reported)
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Oral risperidone: within ~1 hour; metabolite peak varies by metabolizer status
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Active moiety (risperidone + 9-hydroxyrisperidone): ~20 hours on average; prolonged in older adults
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Daily dosing effect is from the combined active moiety with ~20-hour half-life; clinical effects accumulate over days
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively hepatic via CYP2D6 (major) and CYP3A4 (minor) to 9-hydroxyrisperidone (active; paliperidone)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (~70%, primarily as active metabolite) and feces (~14%)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food does not significantly affect rate or extent of absorption

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Risperidone is used for psychosis and mood episodes where reality-testing or behavior is getting hijacked—like schizophrenia or bipolar mania. Clinicians also use it off-label in a few very specific psychiatry situations (severe agitation when psychosis is driving it, or as a low-dose add-on for treatment-resistant depression or OCD). This isn’t a casual med: it can work well, but it can also bring metabolic, hormonal, and movement side effects.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia}: Hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, disorganized thinking, agitation
{link:condition:bipolar-disorder:Bipolar I disorder (acute mania/mixed episodes)}: Racing thoughts, decreased need for sleep, impulsivity, agitation, psychosis
Maintenance treatment in bipolar I disorder (certain long-acting injectable formulations): Helps prevent relapse when adherence is a challenge
Short-term severe agitation when psychosis is suspected to be the main driver (often in urgent or inpatient settings)
off_label: Tourette syndrome (tic reduction in select cases)
Delusional disorder or delusional infestation (specialist use)
Severe or refractory agitation/psychosis in dementia only in rare, high-risk situations after nonpharmacologic options fail (boxed warning applies; not FDA-approved)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Real talk: risperidone can feel like a lifesaver or a hard no, depending on your brain and your side-effect sensitivity. Here are the patterns I hear most:

quotes: The volume got turned down. I still had thoughts, but they weren’t running the show.
I felt less on edge and less reactive—like I wasn’t about to snap 24/7.
My paranoia didn’t vanish overnight, but it stopped feeling like an emergency.

items.category: Sleepiness vs. restlessness (it can go either way)
quotes: It knocked me out at first. I could finally sleep—but I was groggy.
I didn’t feel sleepy… I felt wired and uncomfortable in my own body.
My body wanted to move nonstop. It wasn’t anxiety—it was different.
items.note: Risperidone can be sedating for some people and activating for others (akathisia/restlessness). Either one can tank adherence if it’s not addressed early.

quotes: I felt steadier, but also a little numb.
The highs and lows were less extreme—good—but I also felt less spark.
I was calmer, but I missed feeling like myself.

items.category: Body + hormone stuff (the stuff nobody warns you about enough)
quotes: I gained weight fast and felt hungry in a weird way.
My sex drive disappeared. Like… gone.
My period got weird / I started leaking a little from my breasts and freaked out.
items.note: Risperidone is known for raising prolactin. If you get sexual side effects, menstrual changes, breast tenderness, galactorrhea, or fertility issues—say it out loud early so you can adjust the plan.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Risperidone has two timelines: (1) early calming, and (2) deeper symptom change over weeks. Some people feel sedation quickly; symptom relief for psychosis or mania builds over time.
key_points: Within hours to a few days: Sedation or activation can show up early (and tells you a lot about tolerability).
Acute agitation (oral disintegrating tablet): calming can occur in about an hour in some settings (median ~70 minutes reported).
Schizophrenia: early improvement often within 1 to 2 weeks, with continued gains through 4 to 6 weeks.
Acute mania: initial effects may be seen within days, with ongoing improvement over 1 to 2 weeks.
Long-acting injectable (Consta): meaningful release is delayed—main medication release ramps around ~3 weeks after the first injection, so oral overlap is typically needed early on for some products.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Risperidone is a solid option for schizophrenia and bipolar mania when symptoms are impairing safety, sleep, reality-testing, or functioning. The big clinical win is often reduced intensity—less agitation, less paranoia, fewer hallucinations, and more ability to pause before reacting. The tradeoff is tolerability: weight/metabolic effects, movement side effects, and prolactin-related symptoms are the usual reasons people stop or switch.
sections.clinical_details: In schizophrenia, clinicians often look for early signals in the first 1 to 2 weeks (less agitation, improved sleep, less preoccupation), then reassess more fully by weeks 4 to 6. In acute mania, early calming can occur within days, but the full mood stabilization picture is usually clearer after 1 to 2 weeks. Long-acting formulations can be useful when adherence is the main barrier—but they don’t eliminate side effects, and initiation requires careful planning (tolerability first, then conversion and overlap rules depending on the product).

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Boxed warning: increased risk of death in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Risperidone is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.
sections.black_box: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at an increased risk of death. Risperidone is not approved for the treatment of patients with dementia-related psychosis.
other: Stroke/TIA risk in older adults with dementia-related psychosis has been reported in trials; use only when benefits clearly outweigh risks and non-drug strategies have failed
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): rare but life-threatening (fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability)
Tardive dyskinesia: potentially irreversible abnormal movements with longer exposure; risk increases with duration and total dose
Metabolic risk: weight gain, glucose changes, lipid changes—can develop within months
Hyperprolactinemia: sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, galactorrhea, gynecomastia, fertility issues
QT prolongation: risk higher with other QT-prolonging meds, electrolyte abnormalities, older age, kidney/liver impairment
Orthostatic hypotension and falls: especially during initiation, rapid titration, and in older adults
Severe neutropenia: stop treatment if ANC < 1,000/mm3
Catatonia warning: antipsychotics are not indicated for catatonia and may worsen psychosis and increase NMS risk in catatonic patients
patient_counseling: If you’re older or have medical conditions: start low, go slow, and don’t ignore dizziness or fainting—falls are not a minor side effect.
If you feel inner restlessness (can’t sit still), stiffness, tremor, or facial movements—report it early. Movement side effects are easier to fix when caught early.
Track weight and appetite changes. If weight is climbing quickly, we need a plan (nutrition, activity, labs, or switching meds).
If sex drive tanks, periods change, breast tenderness/discharge happens, or you have erectile/orgasm changes—tell your prescriber. This is common and treatable.
Get urgent care for high fever + severe stiffness + confusion (possible NMS).
Avoid abrupt stopping unless there’s a serious adverse reaction—tapering is usually safer to prevent rebound symptoms.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common themes: sedation or activation (akathisia), movement side effects (EPS), weight gain/metabolic changes, and prolactin-related hormone symptoms. Older adults have higher fall risk and may be more sensitive to blood pressure drops and QT issues.
plain_language_list: Sleepiness or fatigue (or the opposite: restless, can’t-sit-still energy)
Stiffness, tremor, slowed movement, or inner restlessness (EPS/akathisia)
Prolactin-related symptoms (sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, breast symptoms)

common.incidence: Common; varies by dose and individual sensitivity
common.patient_note: Some people feel calmer because they’re sleepier; others feel genuinely less symptomatic without feeling sedated. If you’re too groggy to function, that’s not “tough it out”—that’s a dosing problem or a med-choice problem.

common.incidence: Common; can be misread as anxiety
common.patient_note: This is the ‘I need to move’ feeling—pacing, leg bouncing, skin-crawly discomfort. It can make people quit meds fast. Tell your prescriber ASAP; dose adjustments and add-on treatments can help.

common.incidence: Moderate to high propensity among SGAs
common.patient_note: EPS includes stiffness, tremor, slowed movement, and dystonia. It’s dose-related and more likely during titration. Catching it early matters.

common.incidence: Common; clinically significant gain can occur
common.patient_note: Weight gain can happen fast early on and then plateau, but some people keep gaining. This is a medical side effect—not a willpower issue—so you monitor and intervene early.

common.incidence: High risk compared with many other SGAs
common.patient_note: Think: lower libido, erectile/orgasm issues, menstrual changes, galactorrhea, gynecomastia. If symptoms show up, you can check prolactin and consider dose changes or switching to a prolactin-sparing option.

common.incidence: More common with initiation/rapid titration and in older adults
common.patient_note: Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting when you stand up. Slow titration and hydration help; sometimes you need dose changes or a different med.

serious: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): high fever, severe rigidity, confusion, unstable blood pressure/heart rate (MEDICAL EMERGENCY).
Tardive dyskinesia: involuntary movements (tongue, face, jaw, trunk) that can persist even after stopping.
Cerebrovascular events in older adults with dementia-related psychosis (stroke/TIA), including fatalities reported in trials.
QT prolongation / torsades risk in susceptible patients (electrolyte problems, older age, interacting meds).
Angioedema/anaphylaxis: swelling of face/lips/tongue, trouble breathing (EMERGENCY).
Hyperglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis (rare but serious).
Aspiration risk if severe EPS causes swallowing dysfunction; pneumonia risk increases especially in frail/older adults.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Risperidone is metabolized mainly by CYP2D6 (and partly by CYP3A4). Interactions can raise levels, worsen side effects (EPS, sedation, QT), or increase metabolic and blood pressure risks.

items.risk: Can increase risperidone exposure and side effects (EPS, sedation, prolactin effects).
items.action: Consider lower risperidone doses and slower titration; monitor closely for movement side effects and sedation.

items.risk: Higher risk of QT prolongation and torsades in susceptible patients.
items.action: Avoid risky combinations when possible; correct electrolytes; consider baseline and follow-up ECGs in higher-risk patients.

items.risk: Additive orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, syncope, falls.
items.action: Start low, titrate slowly, monitor orthostatic vitals especially early and after dose changes.

items.with: CNS depressants (alcohol, sedating antihistamines, benzodiazepines, sleep meds)
items.risk: More sedation, impaired coordination, fall risk—especially in older adults.
items.action: Use the lowest effective doses, avoid stacking sedatives, and counsel on driving/falls.

items.risk: Pharmacologic “tug-of-war” that can worsen either psychosis or motor symptoms.
items.action: Specialist management is strongly recommended; choose agents carefully and monitor closely.

items.with: Medications that raise prolactin or worsen sexual function
items.risk: Amplifies prolactin-related side effects and sexual dysfunction burden.
items.action: Monitor symptoms; consider switching to prolactin-sparing strategies if clinically appropriate.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If risperidone is being stopped (because it’s not working, side effects are intolerable, or a switch is needed), tapering is usually safer than stopping abruptly. Abrupt discontinuation can trigger withdrawal-type symptoms and rebound (agitation, insomnia, anxiety, sweating, GI symptoms, dyskinesias, and return of psychosis or mood symptoms). If discontinuation is due to a serious adverse effect, the plan changes—safety first.
key_points: For chronic psychiatric illness, switching (cross-titration) is often safer than a hard stop if symptoms are ongoing.
Common taper approach: reduce gradually over weeks to months; slower tapers are often used after long-term treatment or repeated relapses.
Withdrawal/rebound symptoms can include agitation, insomnia, anxiety, sweating, tremor, GI upset, dyskinesias, and return of psychosis or mood symptoms.

In schizophrenia with high relapse risk, some strategies keep the current antipsychotic stable while the new medication is increased, then taper the old one over 1 to 2 weeks once the new one is therapeutic (specialist-guided).
Long-acting injectables generally have a lower immediate withdrawal risk because drug elimination is slower, but relapse monitoring still matters.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Risperidone dosing depends on what you’re treating (psychosis vs mania vs augmentation) and the route (oral vs long-acting injection). The guiding principle is: start low, titrate based on response and side effects, and use the lowest effective maintenance dose. Special caution is needed in older adults and in kidney or liver impairment.

adult.schizophrenia_initial: 1 to 2 mg/day PO in 1 or 2 divided doses (first-episode psychosis: consider 0.5 to 1 mg/day PO due to higher sensitivity)
adult.schizophrenia_titration: Increase by ≤2 mg/day no sooner than every 24 hours; monitor for akathisia, orthostasis, parkinsonism, sedation
adult.schizophrenia_typical: 2 to 6 mg/day PO (use lowest effective maintenance dose)
adult.schizophrenia_max: 8 mg/day PO (higher doses have more adverse effects and are generally not recommended)
adult.bipolar_mania_initial: 1 to 3 mg/day PO in 1 or 2 divided doses
adult.bipolar_mania_titration: Increase by 1 mg/day at intervals ≥24 hours; in general assess full effect for ≥1 week before pushing higher
adult.agitation_acute_prn: 1 to 2 mg PO; may repeat every 2 hours as needed to a maximum of 6 mg/day (short-term, symptom-driven use)
adult.mdd_augmentation_titration: Increase by 0.25 to 1 mg/day every 3 to 7 days based on response and tolerability
adult.ocd_augmentation_titration: Increase by 0.5 to 1 mg/day every 3 to 7 days (some clinicians titrate more gradually over months)
adult.ocd_augmentation_max: 4 mg/day PO (some patients may need this for optimal response)
adult.lai_im_biweekly_consta_rykindo_initial: 25 mg IM every 2 weeks (some experts start 37.5 mg every 2 weeks in treatment-refractory cases); may increase by 12.5 mg no sooner than every 4 weeks; maximum 50 mg IM every 2 weeks
adult.lai_im_biweekly_oral_overlap: Establish oral tolerability before first injection. After first injection: overlap with an effective oral antipsychotic for 3 weeks (Risperdal Consta) or 1 week (Rykindo).
adult.lai_subq_monthly_perseris_conversion: After establishing oral tolerability: 3 mg/day PO → 90 mg SUBQ monthly; 4 mg/day PO → 120 mg SUBQ monthly. Discontinue oral risperidone the day before the first injection; no oral overlap needed.
adult.lai_subq_monthly_uzedy_conversion: After establishing oral tolerability: 2 mg/day PO → 50 mg SUBQ monthly (or 100 mg every 2 months); 3 mg/day PO → 75 mg monthly (or 150 mg every 2 months); 4 mg/day PO → 100 mg monthly (or 200 mg every 2 months); 5 mg/day PO → 125 mg monthly (or 250 mg every 2 months). Discontinue oral risperidone the day before the first injection; no oral overlap needed.

sections.simple_explanation: Oral risperidone is usually titrated over days to weeks, balancing symptom control against side effects (especially akathisia/EPS, weight/metabolic changes, and prolactin issues). Long-acting injections are mostly about adherence—tolerability is proven first on oral, then you convert using product-specific dose mappings. Some LAIs need an oral overlap at the beginning because the first injection doesn’t fully ‘kick in’ right away.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Risperidone can be used in pregnancy and postpartum when the psychiatric risk of stopping treatment is high, but the decision is individualized. Older adults are more sensitive to orthostasis, falls, QT risk, and cognitive effects. Kidney function matters because the active metabolite is mainly cleared renally.
sections.pregnancy: Outcome data for second-generation antipsychotics as a class do not show a large overall increase in major malformations, but findings for risperidone are mixed and more data are needed. Third-trimester exposure to antipsychotics can lead to newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, feeding issues, abnormal tone, respiratory distress, somnolence, tremor). Tapering late in pregnancy to prevent neonatal symptoms is not recommended; instead, use the lowest effective dose of a single agent and monitor closely. Long-acting/depot antipsychotics are generally not initiated during pregnancy, but may be continued when relapse risk is high and the patient is stable.
sections.lactation: Risperidone and its active metabolite are present in breast milk. Reported relative infant doses are generally in a low single-digit percentage range, but infant sedation, poor feeding, jitteriness, tremor, abnormal movements, and rare respiratory depression (especially in premature infants) have been reported. If breastfeeding while on risperidone, use the lowest effective dose, avoid sedative polypharmacy, and monitor the infant closely (sedation, feeding, weight gain, tone, breathing). Some formulations’ labeling recommends against breastfeeding for extended periods after the last injection (product-specific).
sections.pediatrics: Oral risperidone is used in pediatric psychiatry for specific labeled indications (eg, irritability associated with autism) and for select off-label situations under specialist care. Children and adolescents are at higher risk for metabolic effects, weight gain, and prolactin elevation; careful monitoring is essential. Rapid discontinuation should be avoided due to risk of withdrawal and emergent dystonia/dyskinesia.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid antipsychotics for behavioral symptoms of dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic strategies fail and there is risk of harm. Boxed warning: increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Older adults are also more vulnerable to orthostatic hypotension, falls, sedation, QT issues, and SIADH/hyponatremia. If used for approved psychiatric indications, start low, titrate slowly, and reassess frequently.
sections.hepatic: In liver impairment, free fraction of risperidone may increase (~35%), raising side effect risk (including hypotension). Oral dosing is started lower and titrated cautiously: Child-Pugh A/B often start ~1 mg/day; Child-Pugh C may start ~0.25 to 0.5 mg/day, with cautious titration and longer intervals when higher doses are reached. Long-acting injectable risperidone has limited data in cirrhosis; use caution and prioritize oral tolerability and stability first.
sections.renal: Kidney impairment reduces clearance of the active moiety. If CrCl 30 to 60 mL/min: start ~50% to 75% of usual doses and titrate cautiously (small increments, slower titration), with a maximum that generally should not exceed ~75% of usual. If CrCl 10 to <30 mL/min: start ~50% of usual and do not exceed ~50% of typical maximum. If CrCl <10 mL/min: consider an alternative; if used, very low dosing with careful monitoring. Long-acting formulations require special caution and are often avoided or used only after clear oral tolerability and specialist oversight.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mental status and symptom targets every visit: psychosis intensity, mania severity, agitation, sleep, safety, insight, functioning.
EPS/akathisia every visit (and after dose changes): look for restlessness, tremor, stiffness, dystonia; use a formal rating scale at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk).
Tardive dyskinesia every visit (and formally at least annually): early detection matters because risk increases with cumulative exposure.
Weight/BMI: baseline; at 8 and 12 weeks after initiation and dose changes; then quarterly (more often if rapid gain). Consider waist circumference baseline and annually.
Metabolic labs: fasting glucose or HbA1c at ~4 months after initiation and then annually (more often if abnormal); lipid panel at ~4 months and then annually (more often if abnormal).
Blood pressure/orthostatics and pulse: especially during initiation and titration; monitor for dizziness/syncope and fall risk.
Prolactin: ask about symptoms at every visit until dose is stable; check level if symptomatic (sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, galactorrhea, gynecomastia).
CBC as clinically indicated, especially in patients with low baseline WBC/ANC or history of drug-induced neutropenia; discontinue if ANC <1,000/mm3.
Electrolytes, renal and liver function periodically (at least annually or sooner if medically indicated), especially with kidney or liver impairment.
QT risk assessment: review other QT-prolonging meds, correct electrolytes, consider ECG monitoring in higher-risk patients (older age, heart disease, kidney/liver impairment, polypharmacy).
Sodium in older adults: monitor closely with initiation or dose adjustments due to SIADH/hyponatremia risk.
Adherence every visit; for LAIs, document injection schedule, missed-dose plan, and symptom monitoring between doses.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Risperidone comes in oral forms (including liquid and dissolvable tablets) and long-acting injectables. Formulation choice is usually about adherence, tolerability, and practical logistics (clinic visits, insurance, comfort with injections).
items: Oral tablets: 0.25 mg, 0.5 mg, 1 mg, 2 mg, 3 mg, 4 mg
Orally disintegrating tablets: 0.25 mg, 0.5 mg, 1 mg, 2 mg, 3 mg, 4 mg
Oral solution: 1 mg/mL
IM long-acting injectable (every 2 weeks): Risperdal Consta (12.5 mg, 25 mg, 37.5 mg, 50 mg) and Rykindo (25 mg, 37.5 mg, 50 mg)
SUBQ long-acting injectable (monthly): Perseris (90 mg, 120 mg)
SUBQ long-acting injectable (monthly or every 2 months): Uzedy (50 mg, 75 mg, 100 mg, 125 mg, 150 mg, 200 mg, 250 mg)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Risperidone works mainly by blocking dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. In plain language: it lowers dopamine signaling in pathways linked to psychosis and agitation, while the serotonin effect can help balance symptoms and reduce some side effects compared with older antipsychotics. It also blocks alpha-1 receptors (which can cause dizziness/orthostasis) and histamine receptors (which can contribute to sedation and appetite changes). It has minimal muscarinic (anticholinergic) activity compared with some other antipsychotics.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Risperidone is commonly used for schizophrenia and acute mania because it’s effective and relatively straightforward to dose. Where it gets tricky is tolerability: prolactin elevation and EPS can be prominent, and weight/metabolic issues are real. In practice, it’s a strong option when you need symptom control and the side-effect profile fits the person. Long-acting formulations are especially useful when relapse is driven by missed doses—not because the med is “better,” but because steady delivery helps keep the floor from dropping out.

seo.title: Risperidone (Risperdal): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects, Prolactin, Weight Gain & LAI Options
seo.description: Risperidone (Risperdal) for schizophrenia and bipolar mania: dosing (oral and long-acting injections), onset, side effects (EPS, akathisia, weight gain, prolactin), boxed warning in dementia-related psychosis, interactions, and tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Risperidone is mainly used for schizophrenia and bipolar mania/mixed episodes. It’s also used in some cases for severe agitation (especially when psychosis is suspected) and, at low doses, as an add-on for treatment-resistant depression or OCD.

faqs.q: How long does risperidone take to work?
faqs.a: Side effects like sleepiness or restlessness can show up early—sometimes within the first day or two. For schizophrenia, early improvement often shows up in 1 to 2 weeks, with fuller benefit over 4 to 6 weeks. For acute mania, initial calming may occur within days, with continued improvement over 1 to 2 weeks.

faqs.q: Can risperidone help with sleep or anxiety?
faqs.a: It can make some people sleepy, which can indirectly help sleep short-term. But it’s not a primary sleep medication, and using antipsychotics solely for insomnia is generally not the move because of metabolic and movement risks. If anxiety is driven by psychosis, mania, or severe agitation, treating the underlying episode can reduce anxiety.

faqs.q: What are the most common risperidone side effects?
faqs.a: The big ones are sedation or fatigue (or the opposite—akathisia/restlessness), weight gain and appetite changes, movement side effects (stiffness, tremor, slowed movement), and prolactin-related hormone effects (sexual dysfunction, menstrual changes, galactorrhea, gynecomastia). Dizziness from blood pressure drops can also happen, especially early on.

Yes—risperidone is one of the antipsychotics most associated with elevated prolactin. That can show up as low libido, sexual dysfunction, menstrual irregularities, breast tenderness or discharge, or fertility issues. If symptoms happen, talk to your prescriber early—dose changes, switching to a prolactin-sparing option, or other strategies can help.

faqs.q: What is akathisia and why does it matter?
faqs.a: Akathisia is an inner restlessness—like you can’t sit still and your body is crawling out of its skin. It can look like anxiety but feels different. It matters because it’s a common reason people stop antipsychotics. If you feel it, report it fast—there are fixes.

faqs.q: Is risperidone safe in elderly patients with dementia?
faqs.a: Antipsychotics carry a boxed warning in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis: increased risk of death. Risperidone is not approved for dementia-related psychosis. In rare, severe situations (risk of harm and non-drug approaches failed), clinicians may still use an antipsychotic short-term with close monitoring, but the risk-benefit calculation has to be explicit.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between oral risperidone and long-acting injections?
faqs.a: Oral risperidone is taken daily and is easier to adjust quickly. Long-acting injections (like Consta, Rykindo, Perseris, Uzedy) are mainly about adherence and steady medication delivery. Some LAIs require oral overlap at the start (because the first injection takes time to release enough medication), while others don’t. You still get the same categories of side effects—just with a different delivery system.

Usually, no. Stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal-like symptoms (agitation, insomnia, sweating, GI upset, movement symptoms) and rebound psychosis or mood symptoms. Most of the time you taper. The exception is when there’s a serious adverse reaction—then safety comes first and your clinician will guide next steps.
